title: Building team alignment through structure, systems and interaction
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Team leaders taking over a crew or finding that a crew does not work well together.
learningOutcomes: Diagnose a crew problem at the structural, systematic or interactional level.
Explain why trust is needed for a crew to make hard calls under pressure.
Choose one practical fix for a misalignment and record how it will be checked.

instruction.heading: Alignment and trust
instruction.body: A crew is aligned when its members understand their roles, agree on how the work gets done and communicate openly. Trust sits underneath all three. When people do not trust each other or the lead, they hide problems, protect themselves and avoid decisions. Under pressure, a crew with trust makes difficult calls faster and more calmly.

instruction.heading: Three levels to check
instruction.body: Look at the structure first: who is responsible for what, and do the roles on paper match what happens on site? Next look at the systems: are the checklists, schedules, handover notes and escalation paths in place and used? Finally look at interaction: how do crew members communicate with one another during the shift, and do they raise problems early? A misalignment usually shows up at one level and is caused at another, so check all three before changing anything.

instruction.heading: Taking over a crew
instruction.body: A new lead often meets resistance, sometimes because the crew valued the previous leader or has not yet built confidence in the newcomer. Expect this and do not take it personally. Be steady in applying the agreed standard, communicate the plan clearly, and show through small wins that the crew's effort is noticed. Trust is built through consistent behaviour over time, not through a single speech.

procedure: Describe the symptom in one sentence, for example two workers keep doing the same room.
Check the structure: compare the role list with what actually happens on site.
Check the systems: confirm the checklist, schedule and handover note are current and used.
Check the interaction: observe one shift briefing and one handover and note any gaps in communication.
Choose one fix at the level where the cause sits and state how you will check it works.
Review the fix after two weeks and record whether the symptom has changed.

workedExamples.situation: On a commercial crew of four, two workers keep cleaning the same floor, while the third floor is missed on most nights.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: At which level is the most likely cause, and what single change should the lead make first?
workedExamples.reasoning: The role list is clear, but the room allocation sheet is out of date, so this is a systems problem. The lead updates the allocation sheet, confirms it at the briefing, and checks floor coverage once each of the next three shifts closes.

equipmentAndPpe: Role list, allocation sheet and handover note. Standard PPE on site.

commonErrors.error: Fixing a systems problem by talking to people about attitude.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the three levels in order before choosing a fix.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a new lead's authority is accepted without effort.
commonErrors.prevention: Plan small, visible wins and consistent standards from the first shift.

commonErrors.error: Changing several things at once, so the cause is unknown.
commonErrors.prevention: Change one thing at a time and record the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Changes to roles or rosters can affect pay, hours and entitlements. Check the business's arrangements before changing them.

qualityStandard: The diagnosis names the level (structure, systems or interaction) and the evidence for it.
The chosen fix has a stated check date and a measure of success.
documentationEvidence: Alignment diagnosis note with the three checks.
Fix record with the change made, the check date and the result.
summary: Trust underpins alignment, and a crew with trust makes hard calls faster.
Check structure, systems and interaction in that order before changing anything.
Change one thing at a time and record what happened.

knowledgeChecks.question: A crew keeps duplicating work because the allocation sheet is out of date. Which level is the cause at?
options: Structure, because the roles on paper are wrong
Interaction, because people do not talk
Trust, because people do not like each other
Systems, because the allocation process is not current

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does trust matter for a crew under pressure?
options: It lets people raise problems early and make difficult calls faster
It removes the need for checklists on the job and in the van
It makes the lead's sign-off unnecessary for every task on the site
It replaces the business's procedures for the whole team

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best approach when a new lead meets resistance from the crew?
options: Replace the whole crew at once and hire a whole new team from another city next week
Apply the agreed standard steadily, communicate the plan and build trust through consistent behaviour
Stop giving instructions until the crew agrees and let them decide the work for the day
Set the crew aside and do the work without them and report the problem to the client at once
